claims.say: Updating or deleting a row does not immediately remove the old version.
claims.quote: In PostgreSQL, an UPDATE or DELETE of a row does not immediately remove the old version of the row.

claims.say: A row version is stamped with the transaction ID of the inserting transaction.
claims.quote: The identity (transaction ID) of the inserting transaction for this row version. (A row version is an individual state of a row; each update of a row creates a new row version for the same logical row.)

claims.say: ...and of the deleting transaction, zero if never deleted.
claims.quote: The identity (transaction ID) of the deleting transaction, or zero for an undeleted row version.

claims.say: VACUUM removes dead row versions and marks the space available for reuse.
claims.quote: The standard form of VACUUM removes dead row versions in tables and indexes and marks the space available for future reuse.

claims.say: Transaction IDs are 32 bits and wrap around after more than 4 billion transactions.
claims.quote: But since transaction IDs have limited size (32 bits) a cluster that runs for a long time (more than 4 billion transactions) would suffer transaction ID wraparound: the XID counter wraps around to zero, and all of a sudden transactions that were in the past appear to be in the future — which means their output become invisible.

claims.say: Transaction identifiers are 32-bit quantities and can wrap around.
claims.quote: Transaction identifiers are also 32-bit quantities. In a long-lived database it is possible for transaction IDs to wrap around.

claims.say: IDs are compared in a circle: two billion older and two billion newer.
claims.quote: Normal XIDs are compared using modulo-232 arithmetic. This means that for every normal XID, there are two billion XIDs that are “older” and two billion that are “newer”;

claims.say: A row version looks in the past for two billion transactions, then suddenly appears in the future.
claims.quote: Therefore, once a row version has been created with a particular normal XID, the row version will appear to be “in the past” for the next two billion transactions, no matter which normal XID we are talking about. If the row version still exists after more than two billion transactions, it will suddenly appear to be in the future.

The reason that periodic vacuuming solves the problem is that VACUUM will mark rows as frozen, indicating that they were inserted by a transaction that committed sufficiently far in the past that the effects of the inserting transaction are certain to be visible to all current and future transactions.

claims.say: Frozen rows stay valid until deleted, no matter how long.
claims.quote: Frozen row versions are treated as if the inserting XID were FrozenTransactionId, so that they will appear to be “in the past” to all normal transactions regardless of wraparound issues, and so such row versions will be valid until deleted, no matter how long that is.

claims.say: Every table in every database must be vacuumed at least once every two billion transactions.
claims.quote: To avoid this, it is necessary to vacuum every table in every database at least once every two billion transactions.

claims.say: Autovacuum is forced at the autovacuum_freeze_max_age, even if autovacuum is disabled.
claims.quote: To ensure that this does not happen, autovacuum is invoked on any table that might contain unfrozen rows with XIDs older than the age specified by the configuration parameter autovacuum_freeze_max_age. (This will happen even if autovacuum is disabled.)

claims.say: The forced-vacuum age defaults to 200 million transactions.
claims.quote: Specifies the maximum age (in transactions) that a table's pg_class.relfrozenxid field can attain before a VACUUM operation is forced to prevent transaction ID wraparound within the table. Vacuum also allows removal of old files from the pg_xact subdirectory, which is why the default is a relatively low 200 million transactions.

claims.say: Warnings begin at forty million transactions from wraparound.
claims.quote: If for some reason autovacuum fails to clear old XIDs from a table, the system will begin to emit warning messages like this when the database's oldest XIDs reach forty million transactions from the wraparound point:

claims.say: System refuses new XIDs below three million left.
claims.quote: If these warnings are ignored, the system will refuse to assign new XIDs once there are fewer than three million transactions left until wraparound:

claims.say: In that state running transactions continue; only read-only can start; modifications fail.
claims.quote: In this condition any transactions already in progress can continue, but only read-only transactions can be started. Operations that modify database records or truncate relations will fail.

claims.say: Numbered steps 1-3 (prepared transactions, long-running transactions, replication slots) come before step 4 (VACUUM).
claims.quote: Resolve old prepared transactions. You can find these by checking pg_prepared_xacts for rows where age(transactionid) is large. Such transactions should be committed or rolled back. End long-running open transactions. You can find these by checking pg_stat_activity for rows where age(backend_xid) or age(backend_xmin) is large. Such transactions should be committed or rolled back, or the session can be terminated using pg_terminate_backend. Drop any old replication slots. Use pg_replication_slots to find slots where age(xmin) or age(catalog_xmin) is large. In many cases, such slots were created for replication to servers that no longer exist, or that have been down for a long time. Execute VACUUM in the target database. A database-wide VACUUM is simplest;
